title: An Energy Audit and Search Engines

listening1.context: You are going to hear a conversation between Lamya and Saif.

script.speaker: Lamya
script.text: Hello Saif! The Energy Club has a new project. Mr Said wants us to check how much electricity our school uses. Do you want to be in my group?

script.speaker: Saif
script.text: Yes, please. It sounds very interesting. What exactly are we going to measure?

script.speaker: Lamya
script.text: We will measure how much electricity each room uses in one day. Mr Said gave us a small meter that we put on the plug.

script.speaker: Saif
script.text: Which room do you think uses the most? I think it is the staff room, because there are many fridges and kettles.

script.speaker: Lamya
script.text: I thought so too, but Mr Said says the computer lab uses even more because all the computers and screens stay on all day.

script.speaker: Saif
script.text: That makes sense. What about the air conditioners? Many of them are very cold.

script.speaker: Lamya
script.text: That is another problem. Our school sets them at twenty degrees, but experts say twenty-four degrees is much better. It is still comfortable, and it saves a lot of money.

script.speaker: Saif
script.text: I agree. Can we change the settings ourselves?

script.speaker: Lamya
script.text: We can ask the caretaker, but first we will make a plan. Who will switch off the lights in the classrooms at the end of the day?

script.speaker: Saif
script.text: The class monitors can do that. They are usually the last people to leave.

script.speaker: Lamya
script.text: Good idea. We will also put stickers next to every switch that say, Please turn me off. They are small, but they remind everyone.

script.speaker: Saif
script.text: I can draw the stickers. I will use bright green, so people notice them.

script.speaker: Lamya
script.text: Wonderful. Now, how long will the audit last? A week is too short for good results.

script.speaker: Saif
script.text: Two weeks should be enough. We can compare the numbers before and after the stickers.

script.speaker: Lamya
script.text: Then we have to tell the whole school about the results. Who will we show them to?

script.speaker: Saif
script.text: The headteacher. We will give a short presentation in the morning assembly, with a chart of our numbers.

options: the electricity used by each room
the water used in the school

listening2.context: You are going to hear a talk about how search engines work.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Hello, everyone. Today I am going to talk about something that we all use every day: the search engine.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: There are billions of pages on the internet, and nobody can read them all. A search engine is a tool that helps you to find the right page in a fraction of a second. The most famous one, Google, was started in nineteen ninety-eight by two students in California.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: How does a search engine work? It works in three steps. First, small programs called crawlers, which are sometimes called spiders, travel from link to link across the internet. They visit millions of pages and read them.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Second, the search engine keeps a copy of what the crawlers found. All this information is stored in a huge list called an index. It is like the index at the back of a book, but much bigger. This means that when you type a question, the search engine does not read the internet again. It looks in the index.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Third, the search engine puts the pages in order. It chooses the pages that match your words best, and it also checks other things, for example how many other sites have links to a page.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: You can get better results with a few simple tricks. Use clear key words, not long sentences. If you want an exact phrase, put it inside quotation marks. And if you want to find only recent news, you can choose a date range.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Be careful, though. The first results are sometimes adverts, and they usually have a small label. Also, a page at the top of the list is not necessarily true. Always ask who wrote the page, and when. Websites of schools, universities and governments are usually more reliable than a personal page.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Thank you for listening.

short.q: In which year was Google started?
What are the programs that travel from link to link called?
What is the huge list of stored information called?
What should you put around an exact phrase?

tf.statement: A search engine reads the whole internet again when you type a question.
The first results on a search page are sometimes adverts.
A page at the top of the results is always true.
It is useful to check who wrote a web page.
